To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have observed stimulated emission from all of the molecules listed above.
the energy, time and spectral dependences for the stimulated emission from the ArF*, KrF*, KrCl, XeCl, and XeF molecules excited by a high-voltage fast discharge are reported.

the radiation energy of stimulated emission from ArF* ( λ ≈ 193 nm ), KrCl* ( 222 nm ), KrF* ( 248 nm ), XeCl* ( 308 nm ), and XeF* ( 351 nm ) molecules excited by a high-voltage fast discharge was up to 270 mJ per pulse and the average power reached 0.56 W.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a new type of laser system based on the excitation of the molecules ArF*, KrF*, and KrCl* by a fast discharge and the generation of radiation at the wavelengths λ = 193, 248, and 222 nm.
the development of a high power pulsed excimer laser.
the development of a new generation of compact and efficient lasers, which are based on the use of the stimulated emission of molecules.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in spite of the fact that the ArF* molecule is not very suitable for a laser, it has a number of advantages in comparison with the other molecules.
the results obtained by the author are not in agreement with the results of the previous work.

the results of the experiments reported here are consistent with the hypothesis that stimulated emission in the ArF*, KrF*, and XeCl* systems is due to the radiative decay of the excited states of the molecules.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the stimulated emission from these molecules can be obtained by a fast discharge and that the radiation energy is sufficient for some applications.
the stimulated emission of ArF*, KrF*, and XeCl* molecules is possible in a fast discharge.

the efficiency of the conversion of the energy of the fast discharge into the radiation power of the stimulated emission is 1–10% for ArF*, 0.1–1% for KrCl*, 0.5–5% for KrF*, and 0.05–0.5% for XeCl* and XeF*.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the radiation energy of the KrF* molecules was 0.25 J, which is comparable with the radiation energy of a conventional ArF* laser.
stimulated emission from the above mentioned excimers is possible in the pulsed discharge mode.
the energy of the radiation from these molecules can be increased by several orders of magnitude compared with the spontaneous emission.
